title: CHAPTER TEN. On the Gospel: definition
latin: CAPUT DECIMUM, De Euangelio: ubi de Symbolo Apostolorum. Euangelium est verbum Dei annuncians & proponens omnibus hominibus apprehendendum Christum redemptorem cum meritis suis, & gratis promittens eum viva fide apprehendentibus propter eundem remissionem peccatorum, iustitiam & salutem aeternam. Euangelii, quod proprie significat bonum seu laetum nunciam, definitionem scite proponunt Theologi Leidenses synops. disp. 22 thesibus primis sex, & D. Lutherus. Notat in Theologia bonum nunciam de nato nobis salvatore Luc. 2:10-11 eiusque meritis; speciatim doctrinam de Christo redemptore & gratuita remissione peccatorum propter illum (Matth. 11:5; Rom. 1:16). Alias per synecdochen totam doctrinam N.T. quae etiam legem complectitur (Marc. 1:14-15).
english: CHAPTER TEN. On the Gospel: where also on the Apostles' Creed.

The Gospel is the word of God announcing and proposing to all humans Christ the Redeemer with His merits to be apprehended, and freely promising to those who apprehend Him by living faith remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal salvation for His sake.

Gospel properly means a good or glad message. In theology it notes the good news of the Savior born for us (Luke 2:10-11) and His merits; specially the doctrine of Christ the Redeemer and free remission of sins for Him (Matt. 11:5; Rom. 1:16). Sometimes by synecdoche it means the whole New Testament teaching, which also embraces the law (Mark 1:14-15).
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Gospel properly means a good or glad message. In theology it notes ye good news belonging toward ye Savior born for us (Luke 2:10-11) and His merits; specially ye doctrine belonging toward Christ ye Redeemer and free remission belonging toward sins for Him (Matt. 11:5; Rom. 1:16). Sometimes by synecdoche it means ye whole New Testament teaching, which also embraces ye law (Mark 1:14-15). — Ye Gospel stands as ye word belonging toward God announcing and proposing toward all humans Christ ye Redeemer with His merits toward be apprehended, and freely promising toward those who apprehend Him by living faith remission belonging toward sins, righteousness, and eternal salvation for His sake. — CHAPTER TEN. On ye Gospel: where also on ye Apostles' Creed.

title: Matter of the Gospel: Christ and application of His merit
latin: Continet autem Euangelium tanquam materiam subiectam potissimum duo: 1. doctrinam de Christo salvatore hominum eiusque merito (Rom. 1:3)—ubi dogmata de incarnatione, impletione legis, solutione poenarum, liberatione a maledictione, reconciliatione cum Deo, superatione Diaboli; 2. doctrinam de applicatione meriti Christi, ubi agitur de remissione peccatorum (Acts 10:36, 43), de perfecta iustitia Christi nobis promissa (1 Cor. 1:30), de salute aeterna (Rom. 1:16; 1 Tim. 1:15).
english: The Gospel chiefly contains as subject-matter two things: 1. the doctrine of Christ the Savior of humans and His merit (Rom. 1:3)—incarnation, fulfillment of the law, payment of penalties, liberation from the curse, reconciliation with God, overthrow of the Devil;
2. the doctrine of applying Christ's merit—remission of sins (Acts 10:36, 43), perfect righteousness of Christ promised to us (1 Cor. 1:30), and eternal salvation (Rom. 1:16; 1 Tim. 1:15).
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): 2. ye doctrine belonging toward applying Christ's merit—remission belonging toward sins (Acts 10:36, 43), perfect righteousness belonging toward Christ promised toward us (1 Cor. 1:30), and eternal salvation (Rom. 1:16; 1 Tim. 1:15). — Ye Gospel chiefly contains as subject-matter two things: 1. ye doctrine belonging toward Christ ye Savior belonging toward humans and His merit (Rom. 1:3)—incarnation, fulfillment belonging toward ye law, payment belonging toward penalties, liberation from ye curse, reconciliation with God, overthrow belonging toward ye Devil;

title: Differences between Law and Gospel
latin: Differunt Lex & Euangelium 1. materia: lex praecipit opera; Euangelium annunciat Christum fide apprehendendum, unde dicitur lex fidei (Rom. 3:27) & auditus fidei (Gal. 3:2). 2. Forma: promissiones legis fiunt sub conditione proprii meriti (Lev. 18:5); Euangelii sunt gratuita (Rom. 4:16; Eph. 2:8)—verbum gratiae (Acts 20:24). 3. Effectis: lex terret & damnat (Rom. 3:20; 4:15); Euangelium consolatur & absolvit (Isa. 61:1-2; Luke 4:18)—Euangelium pacis (Eph. 6:15), verbum salutis. 4. Objecto: lex ad impios; Euangelium ad contrita corda (Matt. 11:28). 5. Modo patefactionis: lex natura nota (Rom. 2:15); Euangelium mysterium revelatum per Filium (John 1:18; Rom. 16:26; Col. 1:26).
english: Law and Gospel differ: 1. in matter—the law commands works; the Gospel announces Christ to be apprehended by faith (Rom. 3:27; Gal. 3:2);
2. in form—law-promises under condition of one's own merit (Lev. 18:5); Gospel-promises free (Rom. 4:16; Eph. 2:8);
3. in effects—the law terrifies and condemns (Rom. 3:20); the Gospel consoles and absolves (Isa. 61:1-2; Luke 4:18);
4. in object—the law toward the ungodly; the Gospel toward crushed hearts (Matt. 11:28);
5. in mode of revelation—the law somehow known by nature (Rom. 2:15); the Gospel a mystery revealed through the Son (John 1:18; Rom. 16:26).
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): 5. in mode belonging toward revelation—the law somehow known by nature (Rom. 2:15); ye Gospel a mystery revealed through ye Son (John 1:18; Rom. 16:26). — 4. in object—the law toward ye ungodly; ye Gospel toward crushed hearts (Matt. 11:28); — 3. in effects—the law terrifies and condemns (Rom. 3:20); ye Gospel consoles and absolves (Isa. 61:1-2; Luke 4:18); — 2. in form—law-promises under condition belonging toward one's own merit (Lev. 18:5); Gospel-promises free (Rom. 4:16; Eph. 2:8); — Law and Gospel differ: 1. in matter—the law commands works; ye Gospel announces Christ toward be apprehended by faith (Rom. 3:27; Gal. 3:2);

title: Gospel is not a doctrine of works; summa is the Apostles' Creed
latin: Euangelium igitur non est doctrina operum, ideoque nec nova sive mandata sive consilia legi divinae superaddit. Non esse doctrinam operum patet ex Rom. 10. III. Compendium sive summula Euangelii est symbolum Apostolorum, cuius consideranda est litera, origo & auctoritas. IV. Literam harmonice dispositam sequens exhibet SCHEMA SUMMAE.
english: Therefore the Gospel is not a doctrine of works, and so adds neither new commands nor counsels upon the divine law. That it is not a doctrine of works is clear from Romans 10.

III. The compendium or little sum of the Gospel is the Apostles' Creed, whose letter, origin, and authority are to be considered. IV. Its letter, harmoniously arranged, the following SCHEMA of the sum exhibits.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): III. Ye compendium or little sum belonging toward ye Gospel stands as ye Apostles' Creed, whose letter, origin, and authority stand as toward be considered. IV. Its letter, harmoniously arranged, ye following SCHEMA belonging toward ye sum exhibits. — Therefore ye Gospel stands as not a doctrine belonging toward works, and so adds neither new commands nor counsels upon ye divine law. That it stands as not a doctrine belonging toward works stands as clear from Romans 10.

title: V–VII. Origin of the Creed: baptismal Trinity; later expansions against heresies
latin: V–VII. Symbolum ab initio baptismo in Trinitate ipsa sola consistebat, ut ex Martialem, Ignatio, Justino, Irenaeo, Tertulliano, Origene, Novatiano, & Nicaeno symbolo colligitur. Quotquot in antiquissimis patribus symboli expositiones extant, ultra Trinitatem nequaquam progrediuntur. VII. Quod hodieque est, quantum ad reliquas clausulas, nihil aliud continet quam splendidas quasi vestes primi illius corporis & exstructiones in illud fundamentum, quae suis temporibus necessario addebantur ad haereses exstinguendas & iam necessario retinentur ad impediendum ne recrudescant. Haeretici occasionem dederunt explicationis magis popularis illius symboli quod antea in maiestate quasi silentio complicatum fuerat.
english: V–VII. From the beginning the baptismal Creed consisted in the Trinity alone, as gathered from the earliest fathers and the Nicene Creed. Ancient expositions do not go beyond the Trinity.

VII. What the Creed is today, as to the remaining clauses, contains nothing but as it were splendid garments of that first body and fair structures upon that foundation, which in their times were necessarily added to extinguish heresies and are now necessarily retained lest they break out again. Heretics gave occasion for a more popular explanation of that Creed which before had been folded as in majesty of silence.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): VII. What ye Creed stands as today, as toward ye remaining clauses, contains nothing but as it stood as splendid garments belonging toward that first body and fair structures upon that foundation, which in their times stood as necessarily added toward extinguish heresies and stand as now necessarily retained lest they break out again. Heretics gave occasion for a more popular explanation belonging toward that Creed which before had been folded as in majesty belonging toward silence. — V–VII. From ye beginning ye baptismal Creed consisted in ye Trinity alone, as gathered from ye earliest fathers and ye Nicene Creed. Ancient expositions do not go beyond ye Trinity.

title: VIII–IX. Authority of the Creed; Cap.11 next
latin: VIII. Auctoritas symboli Apostolorum consideratur vel illius quod fuit a principio, vel illius quale postmodum occasione diversarum haeresum explicatum est. IX. Symboli quod fuit a principio auctoritas est prorsus divina & reliquis canonicis scripturis aequalis. Nam immediate est a Jesu Christo Servatore nostro, Matth. 28:19. Sensum articulorum fidei pie docteque enarrarunt e junioribus Lutherus, Melanchthon, Erasmus, Bullingerus, Calvinus, Chytraeus, Hemmingius, Ursinus, Olevianus, Piscator, Perkinsus, Alstedius, alii. CAPUT UNDECIMUM sequitur, De sacramentis in genere.
english: VIII. The authority of the Apostles' Creed is considered either as it was from the beginning, or as it was later explained on the occasion of diverse heresies.

IX. The authority of the Creed as it was from the beginning is altogether divine and equal to the other canonical Scriptures, for it is immediately from Jesus Christ our Savior (Matt. 28:19). Among juniors Luther, Melanchthon, Erasmus, Bullinger, Calvin, Chytraeus, Hemmingius, Ursinus, Olevianus, Piscator, Perkins, Alsted, and others have piously and learnedly expounded the sense of the articles.
CHAPTER ELEVEN follows, On the sacraments in general.
